summary: Abu Moosa Ash'ari told the people of Basrah to weep over their sins and fear of Jahannam, since the people of Jahannam will weep until they cry blood.
Abdullaah bin Abbaas, as Ameer of Hajj, lectured on Surah Baqarah verse by verse, and Shaqeeq said it was so impressive that the Romans and Persians would accept Islaam if they heard it.
Abu Hurayrah praised Allaah from the Prophet's pulpit, foretelling the ruin of the Arabs at the hands of child rulers and that a group from the non-Arabs would reach the Deen.
During the siege of Uthmaan, Abu Hurayrah quoted the Prophet's advice to stay with the Ameer during tribulation and pointed to Uthmaan as that Ameer.
Hajjaaj asks Muhammad bin Yusuf about the narration of Abdullaah bin Salaam, who went to the besieged Uthmaan and addressed the rebels, and the item then passes to lectures of Husayn bin Ali.
notes: Separate reports: Abdullaah bin Salaam at Uthmaan's siege (via Muhammad bin Yusuf), Husayn bin Ali's lecture (via Muhammad bin Hasan), and Husayn's address at Bayda (via Uqba bin Abul Ayraaz). Ends cut off mid-speech after Was Salaamu Alaykum wa Rahmatullaahi wa Barakaatuh with a stray W.

summary: Mujaahid reports Yazeed bin Shajarah urging the people to engage the enemy in full combat and describing the rewards of martyrdom in Jannah.
Mujaahid reports Yazeed bin Shajarah Rahaawi, a governor of Shaam, exhorting the people to combat and describing the recording of deeds, the shore of Jahannam and the punishment there.
Sa'eed bin Suwayd reports that Umayr bin Sa'd, governor of Hims, taught from the pulpit that justice is the wall and truth the door that protect Islaam.
Sa'd bin Ubayd told the people they would meet the enemy and be martyred the next day, and instructed that they not be washed or shrouded in anything other than the clothes they wore.

Salamah bin Sabarah reports that in Shaam Mu'aadh bin Jabal told the Muslims that Allaah would admit into Jannah the prisoners from Rome and Persia who serve them, because the Muslims thank them for their service.
Howshab Fazaari reports that Abu Dardaa feared being asked on the Day of Judgement how he acted on his knowledge, when the verses of Allaah's Book would testify against him.
Abu Dharr asked the Prophet what the scriptures of Ibraheem and Moosa contained, and received lessons and advice on taqwa, the Qur'aan and dhikr, truthfulness, silence and good character.
Aa'isha narrates the Prophet's parable of a dying man's three brothers, representing his family, his wealth and his deeds, and Abdullaah bin Kurz then recited verses on the same theme.
Umar advised a man not to let others distract him from himself, not to waste his days, and to follow each sin with a good deed.
Umar advised staying away from what harms you, keeping righteous friends even though they are scarce, and consulting those who fear Allaah in all matters.

Sa'eed bin Musayyib reports that Umar gave eighteen guidelines, of which only a fragment survives: a principle on responding to someone who disobeys Allaah in matters affecting you, and a verse that only the knowledgeable fear Allaah.
notes: Only a fragment of the eighteen guidelines is given; the text stops after the first guideline and a verse reference.

summary: Ibn Shihaab reports Umar's advice to avoid meddling in others' affairs, to be wary of enemies and of friends who are not trustworthy, to avoid sinners, and to consult those who fear Allaah.
notes: The list of advices is cut off with no closing quotation after the advice to consult those who fear Allaah.

summary: Samurah bin Jundub reports Umar's description of three categories of women and three categories of men, contrasting the chaste, gentle and wise with the demanding and the bewildered.
Umar told Ahnaf bin Qais that laughing, joking and talking too much cost a person respect, make him prone to error, and erode modesty, piety and eventually the heart.
Another narration gives Umar's similar advice on laughing, joking and talking too much, and refers back to the previous narration for the rest.
notes: Variant of n03419; the remainder is given by reference to it, not cut off.

summary: Umar described servants of Allaah who shun falsehood, speak the truth, fear Allaah, and prefer the rewards of the Aakhirah to the pleasures of this world.
Umar advised becoming storehouses of the Qur'aan and fountains of knowledge, asking Allaah for daily sustenance, and keeping company with those who repent often.
Umar said that one who fears Allaah does not vent anger or follow his whims, that justice to people brings success, and that humility in obedience is nearer to righteousness than seeking honour.

Maalik reports Umar's teaching that a man's respect lies in taqwa, his honour in his Deen and his manhood in his character, and Sufyaan Thowri reports Umar's letter to Abu Moosa that wisdom is a gift and that one should avoid shameful acts.
notes: Two separate reports: Maalik's report of Umar's sayings, and Sufyaan Thowri's report of Umar's letter to Abu Moosa Ash'ari.

summary: Umar wrote to his son Abdullaah advising him to hold to taqwa, which Allaah protects, and warned that deeds without intention and wealth without compassion carry no benefit.

Ja'far bin Zabrqaan reports Umar's letters to a governor and to Mu'aawiya bin Abi Sufyaan urging self-reckoning and judgement by the truth, and Ibn Abbaas reports Ali's advice to Umar to curb his hopes and live simply.
notes: Two separate reports: Ja'far bin Zabrqaan's account of Umar's letters, and Ibn Abbaas's account of Ali's advice to Umar.

summary: Ali said that true goodness is not in wealth or children but in growing knowledge and forbearance and in excelling in worship, and that a deed done with taqwa is never small.

Uqba bin Abu Sahbaa reports that after Ali was stabbed by Ibn Muljim, he advised his son Hasan that intelligence is the greatest wealth and foolishness the worst poverty, and to avoid fools, liars, misers and sinners.
Ali said that inspiration is the best guide, good character the best companion, intelligence the best friend and sound education the best legacy, and that only friendship not built on greed endures.
notes: Cut off mid-sentence in the saying about loneliness, followed by OCR debris.

summary: Nimraan bin Makhmar reports that Abu Ubaydah bin Jarraah warned his troops against outward show without sincere Deen and urged them to erase old sins with fresh good deeds.

Sa'eed bin Abu Sa'eed Maqbari reports that Abu Ubaydah, struck by plague in Shaam, advised the Muslims on salaah, zakaah and death, and Mu'aadh bin Jabal then urged sincere repentance and reconciliation with brothers.
Abu Ubaydah said that the heart of a believer changes many times a day, which is why a person should consult others.

Muhammad bin Seereen reports Mu'aadh bin Jabal's advice to give precedence to the share of the Aakhirah over the share of this world, and Amr bin Maymoon Awdi reports Mu'aadh's warning to Banu Awd that all return to Allaah and remain forever in Jannah or Jahannam.
notes: Two separate reports: Muhammad bin Seereen's account of Mu'aadh's advice to a man, and Amr bin Maymoon Awdi's account of Mu'aadh's speech to Banu Awd.

summary: Mu'aawiya bin Qurra reports Mu'aadh bin Jabal's advice to his son to pray as one bidding farewell, and Abdullaah bin Salamah reports Mu'aadh's advice to a man to balance fasting and night prayer, earn without sin, die as a Muslim and beware the curse of the oppressed.
notes: Two separate reports: Mu'aawiya bin Qurra's account of Mu'aadh's advice to his son, and Abdullaah bin Salamah's account of Mu'aadh's advice to a man.

summary: Mu'aadh bin Jabal said that laughing without amusement, sleeping through the night without salaah and eating without hunger expose a person to resentment, and warned that prosperity and women's gold, silver and finery would test the believers.
Abdullaah bin Mas'ood said it angers him to see a man idle, doing nothing for this world or for the Aakhirah.

Ibn Mas'ood said he would not find anyone lying like a corpse at night and restless all day like the Qutrub insect, and that the cream of this world has passed, making death a gift for every Muslim; Ibn Uyaynah explains the Qutrub image.

Ibn Mas'ood compared the world to a drying lake, called death and poverty things people dislike but which a believer can benefit from, and taught that perfect Imaan means preferring halaal poverty and submission to Allaah over worldly honour.
notes: Several sayings of Ibn Mas'ood, followed by his students' explanation of one of them. The lake saying is cut off mid-sentence in the text.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood swore that a person who passes his mornings and evenings as a Muslim will not be harmed by the adversities of this world.

Abdur Rahmaan bin Hujayrah reports that Ibn Mas'ood reminded those sitting with him that lives are shortening, deeds are recorded and death is near, and that each person is a guest whose wealth is borrowed.
